case.label: A
case.text: The strongest case for A: both roles are named in the task definition and both start empty, so a rushed candidate may think the role that the task definition 'runs with' should hold the S3 permissions. It fails because the execution role serves the Amazon ECS agent (image pull, logs), while code inside the container calls S3 with the task role. The phrase 'application code in the container' in the stem points straight at the task role, so the stem itself carries the cue.

case.label: C
case.text: The strongest case for C: baking the agent into each image needs no pod change and the agent then sits with the application. It fails because the stem asks for an agent 'next to' every application container (a separate container), and it forces a rebuild of every image, which is more overhead than adding a sidecar entry. A (DaemonSet) is the habitual Kubernetes answer, but Fargate runs each pod on its own isolated compute, so one node-wide agent pod per node does not exist there.

case.label: C
case.text: The strongest case for C: Amazon EBS volumes can be attached to Fargate tasks and give durable block storage. It fails on two stem constraints: an EBS volume belongs to one task (one volume per task, so tasks do not read and write the same files), and the stem needs a shared set of files across Availability Zones. 'All tasks must read and write the same set of files' is a strong cue that points at a shared file system.

case.label: B
case.text: The strongest case for B: Lambda container images are a natural fit for sporadic, API-started work with no servers, and a candidate may remember a raisable timeout. It fails because the run takes 2 to 3 hours and the Lambda timeout has a fixed upper limit far below that, which a Service Quotas request does not lift. The words 'long-running' and 'does not want to manage servers' are cues that push to Fargate; EKS with a managed node group (A) and EC2 (C) both leave servers to manage.

case.label: B
case.text: The strongest case for B: a Compute Savings Plan applies to Fargate, and the two always-on tasks are steady usage. It fails because the extra tasks change hour to hour and tolerate interruption, so Spot pricing for them saves more, and the plan does not discount the variable part. C breaks the 'two tasks at all times' constraint because Spot tasks can be interrupted. D breaks 'does not want to manage instances'.

case.label: D
case.text: The strongest case for D: a Compute Savings Plan lowers Fargate cost and the 20 tasks are always a predictable size, so a candidate may argue the plan beats on-demand with no interruption risk. It fails because the work is intermittent (a commitment would be paid for while idle) and the stem says the tasks can be stopped and restarted at any time, which is the cue for Fargate Spot. B names an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, which does not cover Fargate.

case.label: A
case.text: The strongest case for A: a candidate may think the task role is 'the role of the task', so the task needs image-pull permissions there. It fails because pulling the image happens before the application code runs, by the agent, with the task execution role. 'Pull the container image' is the cue for the execution role. B violates least privilege and D uses an EC2 instance profile that Fargate does not use.

case.label: A
case.text: The strongest case for A: 'replication' sounds like keeping ECR in step with Docker Hub. It fails because ECR replication copies between ECR registries, not from an outside registry such as Docker Hub. B is the one-time copy that the stem rules out, and D pulls from Docker Hub and so breaks the rule that every image comes from ECR. The sentence 'a one-time copy is not enough' gives away that a rule that syncs upstream is wanted, but it does not name the feature.

answers.flag: Option E also builds the ECR interface endpoints and the S3 gateway endpoint, so E plus C functionally meets the requirements, and the choice of B over E rests only on reading 'least operational overhead' as 'fewest endpoints', although E is a single step.

case.label: E
case.text: The strongest case for E: 'every AWS service that offers interface endpoints' includes the Amazon ECR API and Docker registry endpoints, so it covers the image pull and any logging or secrets endpoint that the stem does not mention, and it is one step to decide instead of picking the right endpoint names. It still loses on overhead and cost (many endpoint network interfaces in each subnet) and is not least privilege on the network, but a careful candidate can defend it as meeting every functional requirement.

case.label: A
case.text: The strongest case for A: EKS Anywhere is the AWS offer that gives the same Kubernetes distribution the teams know and keeps manifests and kubectl. It fails because EKS Anywhere is built to run on customer-managed infrastructure on premises, and the stem says the company wants to migrate to AWS with the least overhead; EKS with managed node groups fits that, while EC2 self-managed Kubernetes (C) keeps the control plane work and a rewrite to ECS (D) breaks 'no refactor'.

case.label: C
case.text: The strongest case for C: the stem does not say that the company can accept a one- or three-year commitment, and 'no commitment' is the only option that has no lock-in, so a cautious candidate may keep standard pricing. It fails because 'steady-state load all day, every day' signals stable usage that a Compute Savings Plan discounts, and 'must not be interrupted' removes Spot (A). The explicit 'no commitment' wording in the options also hints that the answer is the option with a commitment. B names an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, which does not cover Fargate.

answers.flag: Option D leaves out managed termination protection and does not say that the service already uses the capacity provider, so a careful candidate could argue that D alone, or A plus D, does not safely release idle instances, and the 100 versus 50 percent target (D versus E) is a detail that only the numeric target decides.

case.label: E
case.text: The strongest case for E: a target capacity of 50 percent keeps spare capacity so that new tasks start fast when the day peak returns, and the stem never says that idle instances must drop to zero. It fails because 50 percent keeps about half of the group as unused headroom, so the company still pays for idle instances at night, which the stem wants to stop. A candidate who reads 'stop paying for idle instances' as 'reduce' rather than 'remove' could defend E.
